paper_metadata.title: Clock Quantum Monte Carlo: an imaginary-time method for real-time quantum dynamics

experiments.description: FCIQMC applied to a Clock Hamiltonian for a simple quantum circuit consisting of uniform local single-qubit rotations on 11 qubits, used to study the dynamical sign problem as a function of walker population.

algorithm.variant: Clock Quantum Monte Carlo / FCIQMC on Feynman-Kitaev Clock Hamiltonian
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Increase walker population until sign-coherent sampling is reached; observe transition in expectation values versus mean number of walkers.

hyperparameters.observable: Sz of a single qubit at final time
hyperparameters.walker_population_range: mean number of walkers up to ~8×10^5

algorithm.parameter_initialization: Walkers initialized for the history-state simulation; circuit initialized in |0>^⊗N.

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Discrete time register added to the system Hilbert space via the Feynman-Kitaev Clock; each time step is represented by an orthonormal clock state |t>.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Ground-state minimization of the Clock Hamiltonian H = H' + C0 whose zero-energy ground state is the history state encoding the circuit evolution.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Penalty operator C0 fixes the initial state at t=0.
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: Feynman-Kitaev Clock Hamiltonian H = H' + C0

problem_instance.description: Single-qubit local rotation R(theta) applied uniformly across 11 qubits; history state sampled over discrete time.

dataset_specification.description: Quantum circuit instance with 11 qubits and a uniform rotation angle theta = 5π/32.

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Expectation value of Sz at final time plotted versus mean walker number; sign-coherent transition identified visually.

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: sharp transition from sign-incoherent to sign-coherent sampling as walker number increases

speedup_claims.caveats: No explicit classical baseline or speedup factor is reported for this experiment; the result is a qualitative study of the walker-population threshold for sign-coherent sampling.

experiments.description: FCIQMC applied to the Clock Hamiltonian for the same 11-qubit local-rotation circuit, sweeping the rotation angle to study how the sign problem severity depends on circuit parameters.

algorithm.variant: Clock Quantum Monte Carlo / FCIQMC with varying local rotation angle
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Increase walker population until sign-coherent sampling is reached for each rotation angle.

hyperparameters.observable: Sz of a single qubit at final time

algorithm.parameter_initialization: Circuit initialized in |0>^⊗N; rotation angle set per run.

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Clock Hamiltonian history-state encoding of a time-dependent circuit.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Ground-state solution of the Clock Hamiltonian corresponding to the circuit evolution.
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: Feynman-Kitaev Clock Hamiltonian H = H' + C0

problem_instance.description: Uniform single-qubit rotation circuit on 11 qubits, evaluated for multiple rotation angles to compare sign-problem onset and transition sharpness.

dataset_specification.description: 11-qubit circuit with rotation angles 0, π/16, π/8, and 3π/16.

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Expectation value of Sz plotted versus mean walker number for each angle; compare transition location and sharpness.

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: rotation-dependent transition from sign-incoherent to sign-coherent sampling; sharper and earlier for angles closer to quasi-classical

speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports only qualitative dependence of the sign-problem threshold on rotation angle; no classical baseline or speedup factor is given.

experiments.description: FCIQMC with time-dependent local basis rotations applied to a circuit containing local rotations plus a variable number of CNOT gates, testing whether basis rotation mitigates the dynamical sign problem.

algorithm.variant: Clock Quantum Monte Carlo with time-dependent basis rotations
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Increase walker population until sign-coherent sampling is reached; compare rotated versus unrotated basis.

hyperparameters.basis_rotation_scheme: Bt = product of prior single-qubit rotations; two-qubit gates excluded from Bt

algorithm.parameter_initialization: Basis rotations constructed from preceding local rotations in the circuit; circuit initialized in |0>^⊗N.

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Clock Hamiltonian built from rotated unitaries U'_t = B†_{t+1} U_t B_t.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Ground-state solution of the rotated Clock Hamiltonian to recover the circuit history state.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Initial-state penalty term C0; basis rotation used as an error-mitigation / sign-problem mitigation strategy.
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: Rotated Feynman-Kitaev Clock Hamiltonian with U'_t = B†_{t+1} U_t B_t

problem_instance.description: Quantum circuit with local rotations followed by controlled-NOT gates; experiments compare 4 and 8 CNOT gates with and without local basis rotations.

dataset_specification.description: Circuit shown in Fig. 4; controls removed from the end of the circuit first.

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Mean Sz versus mean walker number; compare rotated and unrotated basis for 4 and 8 CNOT-gate cases.

noise_model.mitigation_details: Time-dependent local basis rotations used to reduce the sign problem.

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: rotated basis reaches sign-coherent sampling at lower walker counts than unrotated basis

results.unit: qualitative reduction in walkers needed for sign-coherent sampling

speedup_claims.caveats: The paper shows that time-dependent local basis rotations reduce the walker count needed for sign-coherent sampling relative to the unrotated basis, but does not quantify the improvement as a numerical speedup factor.

experiments.description: Strong-scaling benchmark of the Clock FCIQMC implementation on a commodity Linux cluster, measuring parallel speedup and efficiency for a fixed 11-qubit, 128-time-step circuit.

algorithm.variant: Parallel-in-time Clock Quantum Monte Carlo / FCIQMC
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Run until an equivalent number of statistical samples is reached; compare wall-clock time across processor counts.
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Simulation initialized for a fixed total problem size with walkers distributed across time slices.

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Time-domain decomposition of the Clock Hamiltonian; walkers grouped by time slice for annihilation and communication.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Ground-state sampling of the Clock Hamiltonian for a fixed circuit history state.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Initial-state penalty term C0; time-local domain decomposition for parallelization.
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: Feynman-Kitaev Clock Hamiltonian H = H' + C0

problem_instance.description: 11-qubit circuit with 128 time points generated by consecutive local rotations.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Measure parallel speedup and parallel efficiency versus number of CPU cores; wall-clock time measured to equivalent statistical-sample count.

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: benchmark scaling curves for speedup and efficiency

results.unit: over 2 to 8 processors; exact values not stated in text

speedup_claims.factor: over 95% efficiency with 2 processors; 70% efficiency with 8 processors
speedup_claims.conditions: strong scaling on an 11-qubit, 128-time-step circuit with ~10^6 walkers per time step on an AMD Opteron 6376 Linux cluster using MPI
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper reports efficiency rather than an absolute speedup number in the text; the speedup curve is shown in a figure, but exact speedup values are not stated in the text.

speedup_claims.factor: constant-time nearest-neighbour communication for time-domain decomposition
speedup_claims.baseline_method: general all-to-all communication in interacting-walker Monte Carlo
speedup_claims.conditions: when the number of time steps exceeds the number of processes
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a communication-scaling claim about the algorithmic structure, not a measured numerical speedup.
